cards.headline: One small thing, three kinds of protection
cards.body: Condoms help protect against HIV, other sexually transmitted infections (STIs), and pregnancy. WHO calls this triple protection. They work best when used the right way, every time.

cards.statCaption: protection from pregnancy when condoms are used correctly every time (NHS)
cards.headline: Correct use makes the difference
cards.body: In real life, protection from pregnancy drops to about 82%. Much of that gap comes from how condoms are used, like putting one on late. Good habits close the gap.

cards.headline: Strong protection, not perfect protection
cards.body: Condoms greatly lower risk, but they do not remove it fully. Some STIs, like herpes and syphilis, can pass through skin the condom does not cover. Testing adds more protection.
cards.nanaTip: Using a condom is a way to care for yourself and your partner.

quickCheck.question: When do condoms protect best?
options: Only near the end of sex
quickCheck.explanation: Condoms work best when they are on from start to finish, every time you have sex. Many failures come from late or skipped use.

lessons.title: Putting a condom on, step by step

cards.headline: Before sex: putting it on
steps: Check the date on the pack. Do not use an expired condom.
Open the wrapper carefully so the condom does not tear.
Put it on the hard penis before any genital contact.
If there is a foreskin, pull it back first.
Pinch the air out of the tip.
Roll it all the way down to the base.

cards.headline: After sex: taking it off
steps: Hold the condom at the base.
Pull out while still holding it.
Take it off carefully.
Throw it in the trash.
Use a new condom every time. Never reuse one.

cards.headline: Practice makes it easy
cards.body: Many people feel unsure the first few times. That is normal. You can practise alone, with no pressure, so it feels easy when it matters.
cards.nanaTip: Practice is part of protection.

quickCheck.question: When should the condom go on?
quickCheck.explanation: Put it on before the penis touches a partner's genitals, mouth or anus. Putting it on late is one of the most common mistakes worldwide.

cards.statCaption: from 14 countries were reviewed on condom mistakes (Sanders et al., 2012)
cards.headline: Mistakes are common everywhere
cards.body: A global review found that condom mistakes happen in every country studied. This is normal. Knowing the common mistakes helps you avoid them.

cards.headline: The most common mistakes
steps: Putting it on late, or taking it off early
Not leaving space at the tip
Not pinching the air out
Putting it on upside down
Not using water-based lube
Pulling out the wrong way

cards.headline: Breaks are not the biggest problem
cards.body: Breaks and slips get the most attention. But the review found that other mistakes, like late use, happen much more often. Most of them are easy to fix once you know them.
cards.nanaTip: If a condom breaks, act soon. The next lessons show you what to do.

quickCheck.question: Which of these is a common condom mistake?
options: Pinching air out of the tip
Putting it on after sex has started
Holding the base when pulling out
quickCheck.explanation: Putting a condom on late leaves time without protection. Pinching the tip and holding the base are the right steps.

lessons.title: Lube, oils and doubling up

cards.headline: Use water- or silicone-based lube
cards.body: Lube helps stop a condom from breaking or slipping off. Choose a water-based or silicone-based lube. Anal sex usually needs more lube, because the anus makes little natural wetness.

cards.headline: Keep oil away from latex
cards.body: Oil can weaken latex and make a condom break. This includes baby oil, body lotion, petroleum jelly and cooking oil, such as coconut oil.
cards.nanaTip: Not sure what is in it? Check the label for the word water or silicone.

cards.headline: One condom is enough
cards.body: Two condoms at once do not give double protection. Doubling up can make one or both split. Use one condom, the right way, every time.

quickCheck.question: Which lube is safe with latex condoms?
quickCheck.explanation: Water-based or silicone-based lube is safe with latex. Oils and lotions can weaken latex and cause breaks.

lessons.localNote: Coconut oil is named as a locally common example of a cooking oil; sources name cooking oil in general. Reviewer to confirm which oils and lotions are most often used as lube in Bali.

lessons.title: Keeping condoms safe in the heat

cards.headline: Heat and rubbing damage condoms
cards.body: Heat and friction can damage condoms. That is why a wallet or back pocket is not a good place for them. Health guidance says to store condoms below 40°C, out of direct sun.

cards.headline: Hot spots to avoid
cards.body: Avoid places that can get very hot, like a parked car, a motorbike seat box, or a bag left in the sun. A cool, dry, shaded place is best.
cards.nanaTip: Keep your Nana case somewhere cool and shaded too.

cards.headline: Quick check before you use one
steps: Check the expiry date.
Check the wrapper is not torn or open.
If the pack looks damaged, brittle or discoloured, use a new one.

quickCheck.question: Where is the best place to keep condoms?
options: In a cool, dry, shaded place
In a motorbike seat box in the sun
quickCheck.explanation: Heat and friction can weaken condoms. A cool, dry, shaded place keeps them working well.

lessons.localNote: The motorbike seat box example is inferred from general heat guidance (store below 40°C, out of direct sun). Temperatures inside parked cars or motorbike compartments in Bali were not measured. Reviewer to confirm the example is appropriate.

lessons.title: If a condom breaks or slips off

cards.headline: Stay calm. You have options.
cards.body: It happens. If a condom breaks, slips off, or was not used, there are steps that lower the risk of HIV and pregnancy. Some only work within a time window, so act soon.

cards.statCaption: the latest time to start HIV PEP after a possible exposure (WHO)
cards.headline: HIV: go to a clinic as soon as possible
cards.body: PEP is medicine that can prevent HIV after an exposure. WHO says start it as soon as possible, ideally within 24 hours and no later than 72 hours. Go to a clinic or emergency service.

cards.statCaption: the window for emergency contraception after sex (WHO)
cards.headline: Pregnancy: emergency contraception
cards.body: Emergency contraception can prevent pregnancy when used within 5 days (120 hours). It works better the sooner it is used. Later, get an STI test, because some STIs take time to show.
cards.nanaTip: Save this lesson. You can come back to it any time.

quickCheck.question: A condom broke last night. What is a good first step?
options: Wait to see if you feel sick
Go to a clinic as soon as possible
quickCheck.explanation: PEP and emergency contraception only work within a time window. A clinic can check what you need. Many STIs have no symptoms, so waiting is not a reliable plan.

lessons.localNote: Which Bali facilities give PEP and emergency contraception to the public, at what cost, and whether a prescription is needed was NOT verified. Add verified local service information to the pep help action before launch.

cards.statCaption: curable STIs are picked up every day worldwide, in people aged 15 to 49 (WHO)
cards.headline: STIs are very common
cards.body: Sexually transmitted infections (STIs) pass from person to person during sex. They are common health problems. Having one does not make anyone bad or dirty.

cards.headline: Many STIs can be cured
cards.body: Chlamydia, gonorrhoea, syphilis and trichomoniasis can be cured with the right medicine. Herpes and HIV cannot be cured yet, but medicine can manage them.

cards.headline: Treating early matters
cards.body: Untreated STIs can pass to partners. Some STIs, like herpes, gonorrhoea and syphilis, also raise the chance of getting HIV. Testing and treatment break the chain.
cards.nanaTip: Caring about STIs is caring about your future self.

quickCheck.question: Which STI can be cured with medicine?
quickCheck.explanation: Chlamydia can be cured. Herpes and HIV cannot be cured yet, but treatment helps people stay well.

cards.headline: You cannot tell by how you feel
cards.body: Most STIs have no symptoms. A person can feel fine, look healthy, and still have an STI. They can pass it on without knowing.

cards.headline: Signs to get checked
steps: Unusual discharge from the vagina, penis or anus
Pain when you pee
Sores, blisters, warts or rashes
Itching around the genitals or anus
cards.body: If you notice any of these, get checked. No signs? A test is still the only way to know.

cards.headline: Until you are checked
cards.body: If you have signs, or think you were exposed, use a condom or avoid sex until you are tested. If you are treated, wait until you and your partner finish treatment.
cards.nanaTip: Getting checked is a calm, normal thing to do.

quickCheck.question: Your partner looks and feels healthy. Can they still have an STI?
options: Only if they have many partners
Yes, most STIs have no symptoms
quickCheck.explanation: Most STIs have no symptoms. Looking or feeling healthy does not tell you anything. Testing does.

cards.headline: Vaginal, anal and oral sex
cards.body: STIs can pass through vaginal, anal and oral sex. Oral sex is not risk-free. Some STIs can also pass from a pregnant person to their baby.

cards.headline: Some STIs spread skin to skin
cards.body: Herpes, HPV and syphilis can spread through skin contact. A condom only protects the skin it covers. So condoms lower the risk of these STIs, but do not remove it.

cards.headline: Condoms still help a lot
cards.body: WHO says condoms, used correctly every time, are one of the most effective ways to prevent STIs, including HIV. Vaccines for HPV and hepatitis B add more protection.
cards.nanaTip: Lower risk is still a real win.

quickCheck.question: Why can herpes sometimes spread even with a condom?
options: It can spread from skin the condom does not cover
quickCheck.explanation: Herpes spreads through skin contact. A condom protects the skin it covers, so it lowers the risk but cannot remove it.

lessons.title: Getting treated the right way

cards.headline: A test first, then the right medicine
cards.body: Different STIs need different medicines. Guessing from symptoms can miss the real infection. A health worker can test you and give the right treatment.

cards.headline: Gonorrhoea is getting harder to treat
cards.body: WHO reports that gonorrhoea is becoming resistant to many antibiotics. Using the right medicine, from a health worker, in the way they explain, helps keep treatment working.

cards.headline: Partners need care too
cards.body: If you have an STI, your partners may need testing and treatment too. This stops it from passing back to you. Avoid sex until you both finish treatment.
cards.nanaTip: Telling a partner is hard. It is also an act of care.

quickCheck.question: You were treated for an STI. When is it OK to have sex again?
options: After you and your partner finish treatment
As soon as symptoms go away
quickCheck.explanation: Wait until you and your partner have both finished treatment. A health worker can tell you when it is safe. Symptoms going away does not always mean the infection is gone.

lessons.localNote: Self-treatment with antibiotics bought without a test may be common locally, but no local source was found. Reviewer to confirm whether a local-specific note on self-medication is needed.

lessons.title: How HIV spreads, and how it does not

cards.headline: How HIV passes
cards.body: HIV passes through certain body fluids: blood, semen, vaginal fluids and breast milk. Most people get HIV through anal or vaginal sex without protection, or by sharing needles.

cards.headline: How HIV does not pass
cards.body: You cannot get HIV from hugging, shaking hands, or sharing food, drinks or plates. HIV does not pass through saliva. Closed-mouth kissing does not pass HIV.
cards.nanaTip: Facts protect people from fear, and from unfair treatment.

cards.headline: Many tools prevent HIV
cards.body: Condoms, PEP, PrEP and HIV treatment all lower the risk of HIV. You will learn about each one in this track.

quickCheck.question: Which of these can pass HIV?
quickCheck.explanation: HIV passes through certain body fluids, mostly during sex without protection or by sharing needles. Meals and hugs do not pass HIV.

lessons.title: HIV treatment and U=U

cards.headline: HIV can be managed with treatment
cards.body: There is no cure for HIV yet. But HIV medicine, called ART, keeps the virus under control. Starting treatment early helps protect a person's health.

cards.headline: Undetectable means it does not pass by sex
cards.body: When treatment lowers HIV so far that a test cannot find it, the person cannot pass HIV to sexual partners. Only a viral load test can confirm this.

cards.headline: HIV medicine is free in Indonesia
cards.body: Indonesia's Ministry of Health has said HIV medicine is free at Puskesmas and government hospitals for people in its programme.
cards.nanaTip: Knowing your status early opens the door to care.

quickCheck.question: What does U=U mean?
options: HIV can be cured in a few weeks
Undetectable HIV does not pass through sex
quickCheck.explanation: U=U means a person with HIV whose viral load is undetectable cannot pass HIV through sex. It is about HIV only. Condoms still protect against other STIs and pregnancy.

lessons.localNote: Free HIV medicine at Puskesmas and government hospitals is based on a Kemenkes official quoted by ANTARA (Nov 2023), not a primary Kemenkes page. Confirm with Kemenkes or Dinas Kesehatan Provinsi Bali before launch.

lessons.title: PEP: the 72-hour window

cards.headline: PEP is emergency HIV medicine
cards.body: PEP means post-exposure prophylaxis. It is HIV medicine taken after a possible exposure, such as sex without a condom, a broken condom, or sexual assault. It can prevent HIV.

cards.statCaption: PEP must start within 72 hours. Sooner is better. (WHO)
cards.headline: Every hour counts
cards.body: WHO says to start PEP as soon as possible, ideally within 24 hours and no later than 72 hours after exposure. Do not wait for symptoms or for a test.

cards.headline: Where to go
cards.body: Go to a clinic, hospital or emergency service as soon as possible. You can say: "I may have been exposed to HIV. I need PEP." A health worker will check if PEP is right for you.
cards.nanaTip: You do not need to explain everything. Just ask for PEP.

quickCheck.question: When should PEP start?
options: As soon as possible, within 72 hours
Only after a positive HIV test
quickCheck.explanation: PEP works best when started as soon as possible, and no later than 72 hours after exposure. Go to a clinic or emergency service right away.

lessons.localNote: Which facilities in Bali give PEP to members of the public (not only health workers), at what cost, and outside office hours was NOT verified. Required before launch: verified PEP locations for the pep help action.

lessons.title: PrEP: HIV prevention before sex

cards.headline: PrEP is taken before exposure
cards.body: PrEP means pre-exposure prophylaxis. It is HIV medicine that HIV-negative people use before a possible exposure, to lower their chance of getting HIV.

cards.headline: Different forms exist
cards.body: WHO lists several forms of PrEP: pills, a vaginal ring, and long-acting injections. A health worker can tell you which ones are available and if PrEP fits your life.

cards.headline: PrEP does not stop other STIs
cards.body: PrEP protects against HIV only. It does not prevent other STIs or pregnancy. That is why WHO advises using condoms with PrEP.
cards.nanaTip: PEP is for after. PrEP is for before.

quickCheck.question: What does PrEP protect against?
quickCheck.explanation: PrEP lowers the risk of HIV only. Condoms are still needed to lower the risk of other STIs and pregnancy.

lessons.localNote: PrEP in Indonesia appears limited to selected facilities and key populations (secondary sources only; the Kemenkes PrEP guideline was not opened). Verify eligibility, available forms and Bali sites before launch.

cards.headline: Testing is the only way to know
cards.body: Most STIs, and HIV, can have no symptoms. A test is the only way to know for sure. Knowing early means treatment can start early.

cards.headline: Testing is a normal health check
cards.body: Getting tested does not mean you did something wrong. It is a way to take care of yourself and the people you are close to.
cards.nanaTip: Testing is self-care, not a confession.

cards.headline: Your test, your choice, your privacy
cards.body: You have the right to voluntary, informed and confidential testing. You do not have to tell anyone your HIV status.

quickCheck.question: When is an STI or HIV test a good idea?
options: After sex without a condom, or if one broke
quickCheck.explanation: Most STIs have no symptoms, so waiting to feel sick is not reliable. Testing after a possible exposure helps you get care early.

lessons.title: Test timing and results

cards.headline: Some tests need time
cards.body: After an exposure, the body may need time before a test can find an infection. Some STIs can take up to 7 weeks to show on a test. A clinic can tell you the best day to test.

cards.headline: HIV test timing
cards.body: HIV antibodies usually show within 28 days. WHO says that after a recent exposure, a negative result should be checked with another test after 28 days. Within 72 hours, ask about PEP first.

cards.headline: If a result is positive
cards.body: A positive rapid test or self-test needs a confirmation test by a health worker. If it is confirmed, treatment is available. You are not alone.
cards.nanaTip: One result is one step. Care comes next.

quickCheck.question: You had a possible HIV exposure last week and tested negative. What next?
options: You are sure to be HIV-negative
You never need to test again
quickCheck.explanation: A test soon after an exposure can miss HIV. WHO advises testing again after 28 days.

lessons.localNote: The 7-week STI figure is from NHS (UK). Reviewer to confirm it matches tests used at Indonesian facilities.

lessons.title: Where to get tested in Indonesia

cards.headline: Start at a Puskesmas
cards.body: A Puskesmas is a government community health centre. Indonesia's Ministry of Health has said HIV tests are free at thousands of health facilities, including Puskesmas.

cards.headline: What you can ask for
cards.body: You can ask for an HIV test, an STI check, or advice after a broken condom. The Ministry of Health says HIV testing is also offered at hospitals, clinics and community services.

cards.headline: Worried about privacy?
cards.body: Testing should be voluntary and confidential. You can bring a trusted friend. If one place does not feel welcoming, you can try another.
cards.nanaTip: You deserve care without judgement.

quickCheck.question: Where can you start for a free HIV test in Indonesia?
quickCheck.explanation: Indonesia's Ministry of Health has said HIV tests are free at many government health facilities, including Puskesmas.

lessons.localNote: Free HIV testing is based on Kemenkes statements reported by detikHealth (2018) and ANTARA (2023); expansion to hospitals, clinics and community services from Suara Surabaya (2026). No primary Kemenkes page was opened. Verify for Bali: which Puskesmas offer HIV tests and STI services, cost, hours, ID/BPJS requirements, and how unmarried young adults are treated.

cards.headline: Consent is a clear, free yes
cards.body: Everyone has the right to decide what they will and will not do sexually. Consent means each person agrees, freely. Sex forced through pressure or threats is sexual violence.

cards.headline: What consent looks like
steps: It is given freely, with no pressure.
It is clear and active, not assumed.
It can be taken back at any point.
It is needed from everyone, every time.

cards.headline: Ask, and listen
cards.body: Asking "Is this okay?" is normal and caring. Listen to words and body language. If someone seems unsure, stop and check in.
cards.nanaTip: Respecting a no is part of good sex.

quickCheck.question: Your partner said yes earlier, but now says stop. What do you do?
quickCheck.explanation: Consent can be taken back at any point. When someone says stop, you stop.

cards.headline: Some things block a real yes
cards.body: UNESCO lists things that can affect a person's ability to give or recognise consent: alcohol and drugs, power differences, money problems, and violence.

cards.headline: Too drunk, high or asleep
cards.body: If someone is very drunk, high, asleep or not fully aware, they cannot give a real yes. Wait. Sex can happen another time, when both of you can clearly agree.

cards.headline: Pressure is not consent
cards.body: Begging, guilt, threats, or "if you loved me, you would" are pressure. A yes given because of pressure is not a free yes.
cards.nanaTip: A real yes never needs to be pulled out of someone.

quickCheck.question: Someone is very drunk and says yes. Is this clear consent?
options: Only if you are drunk too
No, alcohol can stop a person from truly agreeing
quickCheck.explanation: Alcohol and drugs can stop a person from giving a real, clear yes. The caring choice is to wait.

lessons.title: Talking about condoms with a partner

cards.headline: Protection is a shared choice
cards.body: UNESCO says deciding to use a condom is the responsibility of both partners. It is not only the man's job, or only the woman's.

cards.headline: Simple things you can say
steps: "I only have sex with a condom."
"I have one here. Let's use it."
"I care about us both. Condom first."
"Not without a condom. We can do other things."

cards.headline: If they refuse
cards.body: You have the right to say no to sex without a condom. A partner who pushes you to drop protection is not respecting you. You can stop at any time.
cards.nanaTip: Saying it out loud gets easier each time.

quickCheck.question: Who is responsible for using condoms?
quickCheck.explanation: Protection is a shared choice. Both partners can bring it up, and both can say no to sex without it.

lessons.title: If something happened without consent

cards.headline: It is not your fault
cards.body: If you were forced or pressured into sex, it is not your fault. It does not matter what you wore, drank or said. You deserve care and support.

cards.statCaption: to start HIV PEP; emergency contraception works up to 5 days (WHO)
cards.headline: Getting care soon helps
cards.body: A clinic or hospital can offer medicine to prevent HIV (PEP) and pregnancy (emergency contraception), and can check for STIs. These work best when started soon. Go as soon as you can.

cards.headline: You do not have to do this alone
cards.body: Bring someone you trust if you can. Health workers should treat you with respect and privacy. You choose what to share, and when.
cards.nanaTip: Your body, your pace, your choices.

quickCheck.question: After unwanted sex, what can help most in the first days?
options: Going to a clinic or hospital soon
Waiting to see if you feel sick
quickCheck.explanation: PEP and emergency contraception work best when started soon. A clinic can also check for STIs and support you.

lessons.localNote: No verified local survivor services (hotlines, hospital-based services, legal steps) are listed. Add verified Bali referrals before launch. Legal reporting options were deliberately left out pending local legal review.

lessons.title: Preventing pregnancy

cards.headline: Pregnancy can happen from vaginal sex
cards.body: Pregnancy can happen when sperm enters the vagina. Condoms and other modern methods, like pills, injections and implants, help prevent it.

cards.statCaption: protection from pregnancy with condoms used correctly every time; about 82% with typical use (NHS)
cards.headline: Condoms give double protection
cards.body: Condoms help protect against both pregnancy and STIs. Pills, injections and implants prevent pregnancy, but do not protect against STIs. Many people use both.

cards.headline: Get advice that fits you
cards.body: A health worker can help you choose a method that suits you. Preventing pregnancy is the responsibility of both partners.
cards.nanaTip: Planning ahead is a kind thing to do for your future.

quickCheck.question: Which method protects against both pregnancy and STIs?
quickCheck.explanation: Condoms help protect against both pregnancy and STIs. Pills prevent pregnancy only. Pulling out is less reliable and does not prevent STIs.

lessons.localNote: Access to contraception for unmarried young adults at Indonesian Puskesmas and pharmacies was not verified. Reviewer to confirm what can be said about local access.

lessons.title: Emergency contraception

cards.headline: A backup after sex
cards.body: Emergency contraception (EC) can prevent pregnancy after sex without protection, or if a condom broke. There are EC pills, and a copper IUD that a health worker puts in.

cards.statCaption: EC can be used up to 120 hours after sex. Sooner works better. (WHO)
cards.headline: Sooner is better
cards.body: WHO says EC pills can prevent most pregnancies when used within 5 days. A copper IUD put in within 5 days is the most effective option.

cards.headline: What EC does and does not do
cards.body: EC is not an abortion. It cannot end a pregnancy that has already started. It does not prevent HIV, so ask about PEP and an STI test too.
cards.nanaTip: Knowing this before you need it makes a hard day easier.

quickCheck.question: What is true about emergency contraception?
options: It works better the sooner it is used
quickCheck.explanation: EC can be used up to 5 days after sex, but it works better the sooner it is used. It does not cause an abortion.

lessons.localNote: Availability of EC pills and copper IUD insertion for unmarried young adults in Bali (pharmacy or prescription, Puskesmas policy, legal status) was NOT verified. Must be checked before launch.

lessons.title: Myth: you can tell by looking

cards.headline: Myth: people with STIs look sick
cards.body: Many people believe someone with HIV or an STI looks sick. This is not true. Most STIs have no symptoms, and people with HIV can look and feel healthy.

cards.statCaption: of unmarried Indonesians aged 15 to 25 had full, correct HIV knowledge (IDHS 2017 analysis)
cards.headline: Many people were never taught this
cards.body: If you did not know this, it is not your fault. Sex education is often missing. Learning the facts now protects you and the people you care about.

cards.headline: The only way to know
cards.body: Clean, kind, rich or religious people can have STIs too. Looks and reputation tell you nothing. Tests tell you. Condoms protect you.
cards.nanaTip: Curiosity is how myths end.

quickCheck.question: How can you know if a partner has an STI?
quickCheck.explanation: Most STIs have no visible signs. Only a test can tell.

lessons.title: Myth: HIV passes through condoms

cards.headline: Myth: condoms have tiny holes
cards.body: A myth in Indonesia says latex condoms have tiny pores that let HIV through. Health experts in Indonesia have rejected this myth for years.

cards.headline: What the science says
cards.body: Lab studies show latex condoms block even the smallest STI germs. In real life, condoms fail mostly because of how they are used, like late use, breaks or slips.

cards.headline: Trust condoms, and use them well
cards.body: Check the expiry date and the pack. Keep them away from heat. Used correctly every time, condoms are one of the most effective protections against HIV.
cards.nanaTip: Good facts beat scary rumours.

quickCheck.question: Can HIV pass through an undamaged latex condom?
quickCheck.explanation: Lab studies show latex blocks even the smallest STI germs, including HIV. Correct use is what matters most.

lessons.localNote: Evidence that the porous-condom myth circulates in Indonesia comes from a 2007 KPAP Jakarta press release. How common it is among young adults in Bali today is unknown. Reviewer to confirm it is still relevant.

cards.headline: Myth: pulling out prevents pregnancy
cards.body: Pulling out before ejaculation is called withdrawal. WHO lists it as less reliable than modern methods, like condoms or pills.

cards.headline: It does not prevent STIs
cards.body: Withdrawal does not protect against HIV or other STIs. Body fluids and skin still touch before pulling out.

cards.headline: A better plan
cards.body: Use a condom from the start. If you relied on pulling out, emergency contraception can still prevent pregnancy within 5 days. For HIV, ask about PEP within 72 hours.
cards.nanaTip: Plan A: a condom from the start.

quickCheck.question: Does pulling out protect against STIs?
quickCheck.explanation: Withdrawal does not protect against HIV or other STIs, and it is less reliable for preventing pregnancy. A condom from the start protects against both.

lessons.title: HIV stigma, and why it matters

cards.statCaption: of unmarried Indonesians aged 15 to 25 showed stigmatising attitudes toward people with HIV (IDHS 2017 analysis)
cards.headline: Stigma is common, and it hurts
cards.body: Fear and shame can make people afraid to get tested or treated. Stigma grows from myths, not from facts.

cards.headline: The facts today
cards.body: HIV can be managed with treatment. People whose HIV is undetectable cannot pass it through sex. HIV does not pass through hugs, food or sharing a room.

cards.headline: You can help
cards.body: Talk about HIV with facts, not fear. Support a friend who wants to get tested. Kindness makes it easier for everyone to seek care.
cards.nanaTip: Every calm conversation chips away at stigma.

quickCheck.question: Why does HIV stigma matter?
options: It can stop people from getting tested
quickCheck.explanation: Stigma can make people afraid to test or seek treatment. Facts and kindness help people get care.
